newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mediterranean states discuss water resources.
newsitem.headline: Mediterranean states discuss water resources.

text.p: Ministers and experts from countries around the Mediterranean on Monday began two days of discussion on water resources, an acute problem for the region of 426 million people.

French government minister Jean-Claude Gaudin, opening the conference which brought together 15 European Union countries and 12 North African and Middle East states, linked a solution of the regional issue to the stability of Europe.
The European Union had been quick "to recognise that the stability and prosperity of the Mediterranean Basin are essential for Europe," he said in an opening speech.
"Water management is one of the keys to this prosperity," added Gaudin, who is France's Territorial Planning Minister and mayor of Marseille.

Water has been singled out as an area of regional cooperation because it is so unequally shared with more than two-thirds of the region's resources concentrated in France, Italy, Turkey and ex-Yugoslavia.
Poorest off in the region are Malta, Cyprus, Jordan, the Palestinian territories and Libya, which was not represented at the meeting.
The conference on Monday was to discuss recommendations for managing water resources for agriculture and industry to the training of a new generation of water technicians.
Tuesday's session was to hear speeches by ministers.

The presence of Israeli and Syrian delegates together at the conference was the first such since the election victory in May of hardline Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and subsequent rising tensions.
The two countries have waged wars in the past over control of water resources.

A spokesman for the International Office of Water, one of the conference organisers, said: "Despite the tensions and current difficulties, dialogue and cooperation can, and must, develop in the interest of all the countries involved."
The groundwork for the Marseille water conference emerged last year when foreign ministers of European and Mediterranean nations met in Barcelona, Spain, to identify possible areas of cooperation.

The total population of the region, now at about 426 million people, could exceed 600 million in 2025 with urbanisation reaching alarming rates and few answers on how to meet food and water requirements.

Distribution is also unequal within countries of the region with 81 percent of Spain's resources concentrated in the north of the country and three-quarters of Algeria's resources concentrated in just six percent of the North African country.
